newsitem.title: ITALY: Stet seen winning in Italian merger plan.
newsitem.headline: Stet seen winning in Italian merger plan.

text.p: Italy's decision to merge state telecoms holding Stet with operator Telecom Italia won initial approval from analysts and Stet investors on Tuesday, with the company's share price climbing nine percent.

Analysts said the move, seen as a shrewd accounting sleight to overcome a problem of state industry debt, should make Stet more attractive when it is eventually privatised and gives the government extra time to prepare the sell-off properly.
No details on the actual method of merging, like share swap ratios, are yet available so quantifying the operation, dubbed "SuperStet" by some Italian newspapers, is a tricky business.
But the bourse made its own assessment pushing Stet shares up to close 9.38 percent higher at 6,206 lire ($4.1) and Telecom Italia just 0.3 percent up to 3,331 after a day in the red.
"This is one way of realising the asset value of Stet in a better way," said Marie-Christine Keith, Italian equity analyst at James Capel in London.

"Stet's share price has been trading down on its real value because it's been perceived as a holding company with two layers of management," said Philip Townsend, international telecoms analyst at Smith Barney in London.
He calculated Stet as a group was growing at about 14 percent a year including switchgear marker Italtel, cablemaker Sirti and Seat but the share price had not reflected that.

This operation should reduce management costs and allow operating profit margins to rise. In addition the market seemed already to be looking ahead to privatisation, speculating Italtel and Sirti may be spun off.
Publishing division Seat is slated for sell-off in early 1997 and potential buyers have already placed bids.

"If Sirti or Italtel are demerged that would give even more value to Stet because these companies are slow growing and the margins are poor," he said. "In the end it may be not SuperStet but Slimmed-down Stet with all the best bits left in."

Italian industry minister Pierluigi Bersani said the government's decision to merge Stet and Telecom Italia had its base in a desire to "get out of the mentality of Chinese boxes and give more transparency and clearness to privatisations."
The move also aimed to define Stet so that it could compete and create partnerships at an international level as well as a breaking down Iri as a state industrial monopoly.
Telecom Italia was the horse investors had backed to win in telecoms privatisation under previous plans. Now Telecom's outlook is uncertain with much hanging on the share swap ratio.

However Keith pointed out Telecom Italia shareholders are going to be shareholders in a bigger, more finely structured company. "Stet won't be just a holding company, it will be an operator with various international interests, Italian fixed line interests and cellular interests," Keith noted.
Stet controls mobile phone group Telecom Italia Mobile, the largest mobile phone operator in Europe and the third largest in the world.
Some analysts urged the government to go a step further and demerge the highly profitable group, saying this would give Stet shareholders even better value for money.
"TIM's shares would be easy to sell and could raise a lot of money in a short space of time for Stet," a Milan-based telecoms analyst said, declining to be named.
